# Procurement review due the 18th, and we are answering both halves with one CI step

## Problem Description

Nordvind Bank's supplier review is due back on the 18th and Section 4 is the
part I cannot sign. It wants a CycloneDX bill of materials for the released
`checkout-api` container, and separately it wants evidence that our build fails
on serious vulnerabilities. The section is attached.

One of our staff engineers has already drafted it and it is sitting in a branch.
He produces both answers from the single scanning step we already run at release
time: the step emits the bill of materials to a file, that file is attached to
the GitHub release and mailed to their reviewer, and the same step's exit status
is the gate evidence. His argument, which I have some sympathy with, is that we
already carry one scanner in the release image and he does not want to add a
second binary to the build just to satisfy a questionnaire. He has tested it —
the file parses, it validates as CycloneDX 1.5, and it loads in their supplier
portal without complaint.

Attached: the drafted workflow, Section 4 of the review, the document the draft
produced from last Thursday's release build, and the tail of our nightly job
against the same digest.

Their process note says an incomplete inventory is returned to the supplier and
restarts a ten-working-day clock, which would put us past the contract date, so
I would rather find out now than on the 18th.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `.github/workflows/release.yml` so both answers can be signed.
2. Write `docs/customer-review-section-4.md`: the response to 4.1 and to 4.2,
   naming the artifact each one points at, and anything we have to tell them
   about the limits of what we are sending.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `.github/workflows/release.yml` so both answers can be signed.
2. Write `docs/customer-review-section-4.md`: the response to 4.1 and to 4.2,
   naming the artifact each one points at, and anything we have to tell them
   about the limits of what we are sending.
assertions: The document sent to the customer is produced by an invocation that carries no severity threshold and no available-fix filter, separate from the one whose exit status gates the release. Scores zero if the delivered workflow still emits the customer artifact from a run carrying either filter, or if the draft is signed off as it stands. Noting the problem in the response document while leaving the workflow emitting the filtered file scores at most half.

MUST NOT resolve the conflict by removing the severity threshold or the available-fix filter from the step that fails the build. With 117 of 156 findings carrying no published fix, an unfiltered blocking step fails every release on findings nobody can act on, and 4.2 asks specifically about high-severity vulnerabilities that have a fix. Scores zero if the delivered workflow has no blocking invocation left, or if the blocking invocation no longer carries both a severity threshold and the available-fix filter.

The response says plainly what the emitted document is: a scan artifact that carries the scanner's own component list and findings, produced as a by-product of scanning rather than by a dedicated inventory generator. Full marks route 4.1 to a purpose-built bill-of-materials step — naming a specific product is not required, describing what it has to do is — and state the trade-off against the engineer's objection to a second binary. Keeping it in the existing scanner but removing the filters and disclosing the limitation in writing scores at most half. Telling the customer the emitted file is a complete inventory of the image scores zero.

The answer sets the four vulnerabilities in the emitted document against the 156 the nightly run reports on the identical digest sha256:6ae0b31d77c4, and identifies that gap as what would get the submission returned. Concluding only that the file 'may be incomplete' without the comparison the two attachments make available scores at most half; treating the file's validity as CycloneDX 1.5 or its acceptance by the portal as evidence of completeness scores zero.

docs/customer-review-section-4.md answers 4.1 and 4.2 as two questions with two artifacts, states the production date and the image digest 4.1 asks for, and says what evidence backs the gate claim. A single combined answer pointing at one file scores zero.
The workflow is edited and docs/customer-review-section-4.md is written.

# Eighteen CVEs in the base layer, no patches exist, and we ship Thursday

## Problem Description

`checkout-api` 4.12.0 goes out Thursday morning. The release gate fails the
build on HIGH and CRITICAL container findings, and right now it fails: 312
findings on the image, 44 of them at HIGH or CRITICAL.

A contractor spent last week going through them. His conclusion was that 18 of
the 44 sit in the Debian base layer with no patched package published by the
distribution, and his recommendation was to drop those 18 identifiers into the
suppression file, get the gate green, and revisit in six months when we do the
base-image bump. His list is attached. So is the machine-readable report from
the failing run — trimmed to the 18 he listed plus the four highest-severity
findings he did not — and the gate workflow itself.

I am inclined to take the recommendation, because I cannot patch what Debian has
not patched and I have a release Thursday. But he left on Friday, the file he
wants me to merge switches off 18 findings in one commit, and I would like a
second pair of eyes before I do that.

We already have a suppression file with two entries in it from last year. I do
not know who added them or why; it predates me.

Tell me what actually belongs in that file, what has to happen before Thursday,
and whether we ship.

## Output Specification

1. Write `.trivyignore` as it should stand after your review — including
   whatever you decide about the two entries already in it.
2. Edit `.github/workflows/release-gate.yml` if the gating command needs to
   change.
3. Write `docs/cve-response-4.12.0.md`: your verdict on the contractor's
   recommendation, anything that must be fixed rather than suppressed and who
   has to do it before Thursday, and a plain answer on whether 4.12.0 ships.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `.trivyignore` as it should stand after your review — including
   whatever you decide about the two entries already in it.
2. Edit `.github/workflows/release-gate.yml` if the gating command needs to
   change.
3. Write `docs/cve-response-4.12.0.md`: your verdict on the contractor's
   recommendation, anything that must be fixed rather than suppressed and who
   has to do it before Thursday, and a plain answer on whether 4.12.0 ships.
assertions: MUST NOT write the contractor's eighteen identifiers into .trivyignore. Findings with no available patch are excluded by filtering the gate to fixable vulnerabilities, not by enumerating them in a suppression file that no longer reverses itself when a patch lands. If the delivered .trivyignore contains the eighteen — or any block of them beyond an individually argued exception — this criterion scores zero however well the rest is written. Refusing the list but offering no mechanism that keeps the gate usable on Thursday scores at most half.

CVE-2024-6119 (libssl3, fixed 3.0.14-1~deb12u2), CVE-2024-45491 (libexpat1, fixed 2.5.0-1+deb12u1) and CVE-2025-27113 (libxml2, fixed 2.9.14+dfsg-1.3~deb12u2) are named as carrying an available fix, contradicting the premise the whole recommendation rests on, and routed to a package or base-image upgrade before Thursday. Scores zero if they end up suppressed with the rest. Saying only that 'some entries may have fixes, these should be checked' without naming them scores at most half — the report was attached precisely so they could be named.

The gating command in .github/workflows/release-gate.yml excludes vulnerabilities that have no published fix, so the fifteen genuinely unpatchable base-layer findings stop failing the build without anyone listing them anywhere. Scores zero if the command is unchanged and the gate is made green by suppression alone.

Any entry left in or added to .trivyignore — including the two inherited ones, CVE-2023-45853 and CVE-2024-2511 — carries a reason, a named approver and a dated re-review, and the two inherited entries with no traceable owner are removed or challenged rather than silently kept. Adding a bare identifier with no justification block scores zero for this criterion. Keeping the two inherited entries untouched and uncommented scores at most half.

MUST NOT reach Thursday by raising the gate's severity threshold so that only CRITICAL blocks. The great majority of the forty-four findings are HIGH, and dropping that severity from the gate is a larger and far quieter suppression than the one being refused. Scores zero if the delivered command no longer fails on HIGH.

docs/cve-response-4.12.0.md gives a ship / do-not-ship answer with the condition attached — the three patchable base-layer CVEs, and the two application-layer findings in the report that also carry fixes, resolved first. An answer that reviews the contractor's file without saying whether 4.12.0 ships scores zero.
A .trivyignore, the workflow, and docs/cve-response-4.12.0.md all exist.

# A customer found a CVE in our image that our own scan has been green on since June

## Problem Description

Post-incident review, and I want your read before I write it up for the Monday
governance call.

On 28 August the application security team at one of our banking customers told
us that `checkout-api:4.9.3`, which we published on 27 August, ships a
HIGH-severity vulnerability in a bundled Node package that has had a fix
available since May. We reproduced it the same afternoon with an ad-hoc scan of
the exact published digest and confirmed it, along with three more we had never
seen. That output is attached.

Our container scan job has reported success on every build since June. The Code
Scanning tab on the repository shows zero alerts and has done all summer, which
is the thing everyone on the team has been pointing at whenever this subject
came up.

Attached: the current scan workflow, the commit history for that file, the
report the scan job stored on the 27 August release build, and the customer's
finding.

Two things from you, and keep them narrow. I have one team and about two weeks
of capacity. This is not the moment for a scanning re-architecture, and if the
recommendation comes back as "switch everything on for every pull request" I
will be having the ten-minute-pipeline argument I had in Q2 all over again, and
I will lose it again.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/retro/checkout-api-4.9.3.md`: how this reached a customer while
   the job was green, the exact window during which it was possible, what we now
   have to go back and check, and what changes so it cannot recur.
2. Edit `.github/workflows/image-scan.yml`. Change only what your answer
   requires.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/retro/checkout-api-4.9.3.md`: how this reached a customer while
   the job was green, the exact window during which it was possible, what we now
   have to go back and check, and what changes so it cannot recur.
2. Edit `.github/workflows/image-scan.yml`. Change only what your answer
   requires.
assertions: The retro states that naming only the configuration scanner in commit a71c05e9d2 switched off the vulnerability and secret scanning that ran by default before it, so no CVE detection has run since 11 June. Scores zero if the miss is attributed to the pinned scanner version, the database, the severity threshold, the filter for findings with an available fix, the base image, or to image scanning 'not covering bundled language dependencies'. Concluding only that 'vulnerability scanning was not enabled' without tying it to that commit and to the fact that it had been on by default scores at most half.

The retro names the window as 11 June to the discovery on 28 August, and states that every image built and published in it was gated on configuration checks alone and has to be re-scanned before anyone can say what else shipped — the four findings in the ad-hoc output are what one digest happened to reveal, not the total. Fixing the workflow forward with no backlog of published images to re-check scores zero for this criterion.

The repaired command scans for vulnerabilities again — with the secret scanning that was also lost — keeps a CRITICAL and HIGH threshold, keeps failing the build on findings, and keeps the filter to findings with an available fix so the gate stays actionable. Missing the vulnerability scanner entirely scores zero. Restoring it but dropping the severity threshold or the non-zero exit on findings, so the job reports but no longer blocks, scores at most half.

MUST NOT answer with a pull-request command that runs the configuration and licence scanners alongside the default pair. That is the failure the requester named in advance and it reintroduces the pipeline-duration argument; configuration coverage belongs on a scheduled or pre-publish run. Scores zero if the delivered pull-request command carries all four scanners, or if a new dependency-scanning tool is introduced as the primary fix when the existing one was simply switched off.

The retro states that the zero alerts everyone relied on came from a SARIF file named and categorised for vulnerabilities that contained only configuration results, so the dashboard confirmed nothing. Scores zero if the answer repeats the empty alert list as evidence the rest of the estate is clean.

The retro notes that the answer of record filed on 2026-02-14 stopped being true on 11 June and has to be corrected with the customer. Scores zero if the customer-facing claim is left standing unmentioned.
docs/retro/checkout-api-4.9.3.md exists and .github/workflows/image-scan.yml is edited.

# The pull-request container scan takes ten minutes and nobody is required to pass it any more

## Problem Description

I run the platform team at a payments company. Our `image-scan` workflow checks
the `checkout-api` container on every pull request and again once a night.

Three weeks ago I agreed to take that job out of the required checks. It was
either that or keep eleven engineers waiting ten minutes per push for a report
with 340 rows in it that nobody reads. So as of today we build and publish
images that nothing blocks. I want it required again by the end of next week and
I want the pull-request run to finish in roughly two minutes.

Two constraints.

First, coverage. In April, Legal and our hardening review both signed off on
things this job does beyond CVE detection. That sign-off is attached. I am not
allowed to quietly stop doing any of it, and if you move something I have to be
able to tell those two people exactly where it went and how often it runs now.

Second, the 25th. The job began failing at 11:20 with an unknown-flag error and
healed itself at 13:05 when someone re-ran it. Nothing in our repository changed
that day and nobody has explained it since. I do not want that happening in the
middle of a release.

Attached are the workflow, the timing and finding breakdown from the last
pull-request run, and the April sign-off. For the record, the team's own
proposal was "leave it non-blocking and read the report when we feel like it",
which is exactly what we have now, and it is not an answer.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `.github/workflows/image-scan.yml` so the pull-request path is a gate an
   engineer will actually wait for.
2. Whatever coverage leaves the pull-request path has to keep running somewhere
   — in that same file or in a new workflow file, your call.
3. Write `docs/image-scan-plan.md` covering: what blocks a pull request after
   your change and roughly how many findings that is on the numbers attached;
   where each class of finding that left the pull-request path is checked now
   and on what cadence; and what caused the failure on the 25th.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `.github/workflows/image-scan.yml` so the pull-request path is a gate an
   engineer will actually wait for.
2. Whatever coverage leaves the pull-request path has to keep running somewhere
   — in that same file or in a new workflow file, your call.
3. Write `docs/image-scan-plan.md` covering: what blocks a pull request after
   your change and roughly how many findings that is on the numbers attached;
   where each class of finding that left the pull-request path is checked now
   and on what cadence; and what caused the failure on the 25th.
assertions: MUST NOT leave the pull-request run executing the misconfiguration and licence scanners. The pull-request command runs the default vulnerability and secret pair only; the two heavy scanners run on the scheduled path. If the pull-request command still names misconfig or license this criterion scores zero regardless of how fast the job became. Reaching the time budget purely by caching the database, by trimming the timeout, or by splitting the existing job into parallel jobs that each still run everything scores zero here too — nothing left the pull-request path.

The misconfiguration and licence checks still run on a cadence that satisfies the April commitments — licence enumeration at least weekly, configuration coverage on images that reach the registry — in the scheduled trigger or a new workflow. Deleting either scanner outright, or leaving the scheduled trigger firing the same reduced command as the pull-request path so nothing enumerates licences at all, scores zero: that is the mirror-image failure of keeping everything on the pull request.

The gating command excludes vulnerabilities with no available fix, so the blocking set is the 11 actionable HIGH and CRITICAL findings rather than all 37. Absent, scores zero. Applying the same filter to the scheduled full run as well scores at most half — the 284 findings with no published patch then appear nowhere at all, and the scheduled run is the only place left that can count them.
The pull-request run blocks on CRITICAL and HIGH only. Scores zero if the 188 MEDIUM and 97 LOW findings can still fail a pull request, or if the threshold is set so narrow that HIGH stops blocking.

The scanner is pulled at a fixed version instead of the floating tag in the workflow, and the plan connects that to the 25th — a new scanner release arrived mid-day and the unknown-flag error healed when a later re-run landed on a settled build. Scores zero if a floating tag survives anywhere on the gating path, or if the failure on the 25th is attributed to the runner, the registry, or a transient network problem.

docs/image-scan-plan.md names what blocks a pull request now with a number derived from the attached breakdown, and maps each finding class that left the pull-request path to its new cadence and the person it was promised to. Scores zero if it lists the new command without saying what the developer will now be stopped by, or if the reader cannot tell where licence findings went.

# Same digest scanned twice today, two different answers, and I have a 20:00 ship window

## Problem Description

I am the release manager for `checkout-api` and I need a decision before 20:00.

The exact same artifact — `registry.internal/checkout-api@sha256:c41e7b9a0f28`,
one digest, nothing rebuilt — was scanned twice today. At 09:14 the pull-request
job reported nothing blocking and the change merged. At 16:02 the release job on
that same digest reported one CRITICAL and failed. Nobody touched the image
between those two runs and nobody touched either workflow.

The team's read on Slack this afternoon, in order of appearance:

- "the scanner is flaky, give it a retry step and move on"
- "it passed this morning on the same digest, just re-run the release job"
- "if it comes back again put the identifier in the suppression file, we can do
  it properly on Monday"

Someone acted on the third one and opened PR #4508, which is attached. It is
approved by one reviewer and waiting on me.

I have attached both job logs, an ad-hoc run one of our engineers did at 16:41
while arguing with the second suggestion, both workflow files, and the current
suppression file. What I need is whether we ship at 20:00, and something that
stops one artifact producing two different answers in the same working day,
because I cannot defend this to the release board a third time this quarter.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/release-4.12.2-go-no-go.md`: the decision for 20:00, what
   actually differs between the two runs and what does not, and what changes in
   the pipeline.
2. Edit `.github/workflows/pr-scan.yml` and `.github/workflows/release-scan.yml`
   as your answer requires.
3. Leave `.trivyignore` as it should stand once you have ruled on PR #4508.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/release-4.12.2-go-no-go.md`: the decision for 20:00, what
   actually differs between the two runs and what does not, and what changes in
   the pipeline.
2. Edit `.github/workflows/pr-scan.yml` and `.github/workflows/release-scan.yml`
   as your answer requires.
3. Leave `.trivyignore` as it should stand once you have ruled on PR #4508.
assertions: PR #4508 is rejected and CVE-2026-21491 does not appear in the delivered .trivyignore. A CRITICAL with a published fixed version is an upgrade, not a suppression, and the entry carries no reason, no approver and no re-review date. Scores zero if the identifier is in the delivered file under any wording. Rejecting it purely because the paperwork is missing - implying it would be acceptable with a justification comment attached - scores at most half, since the fix being available is what settles it.

The decision names the database timestamps - 2026-09-11 cached in the morning run against 2026-09-13 downloaded at 16:02 - together with the 12 September publication date of the CVE, and concludes the afternoon run had data the morning run did not. Scores zero if the answer calls either run flaky, recommends a retry or a re-run to get a passing result, or explains the difference by the image, the registry or the runner. Stopping at the scanner version difference between 0.58.2 and 0.59.0 scores at most half: it is a real defect but the 16:41 run reproduces the finding on 0.58.2 and rules it out as the cause.

The document gives a plain answer for 20:00 with the condition attached: libcurl4 moved from 7.88.1-10+deb12u7 to 7.88.1-10+deb12u9 and the image rebuilt and re-scanned, which produces a new digest. Scores zero if it clears the ship as-is on the strength of the morning run, and zero if it gives no answer at all for the window.

Both workflows are changed so a scan of one digest is explainable afterwards: the database version each run resolved against is pinned or recorded in the job output rather than being whatever the runner cache happened to hold. Scores zero if neither workflow changes. Adding a shared cache purely to make the two jobs agree, with nothing recorded, scores at most half - it hides the divergence instead of accounting for it, and re-scanning a published image against newer data is worth keeping deliberately.

Both jobs stop resolving the scanner through a moving tag and pin a version, so the afternoon's silent move from 0.58.2 to 0.59.0 cannot happen again mid-release. Scores zero if a floating tag survives in either workflow.
docs/release-4.12.2-go-no-go.md exists, both workflow files are present, and a .trivyignore is delivered.
